endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: It is vital to have qualified health care personnel in the loop, and patient/caregiver representatives when they may be end users.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: When relevant, list the qualifications or clinical role of the users intended to 383 interpret the output.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Is the defined problem consistent with goals, user needs, and risk tolerances?

endorsements.title: Alignment of Policy, Practice, and Patient Safety for Trustworthy AI in Radiology
endorsements.quote: Postmarket oversight requirements should explicitly specify which clinician types are qualified to use imaging-related AI tools.

endorsements.title: Mitigated deployment strategy for ethical AI in clinical settings
endorsements.quote: In a dermatology context, the human-in-the-loop should be a consultant dermatologist rather than trainee or generalist.

endorsements.title: Practical consequences of the European union-AI act for anatomic pathology laboratories a European society of pathology and European society of digital and integrative pathology commissioned expert opinion paper
endorsements.issuer: Virchows Archiv : an international journal of pathology
endorsements.quote: In pathology labs, this includes ensuring that AI systems are used strictly in accordance with provided instructions for use, that qualified personnel remain responsible for supervising the AI’s clinical application, and that input data used for using the AI model is relevant and representative.

evidence.title: Value of clinical review for AI-guided deep vein thrombosis diagnosis with ultrasound imaging by non-expert operators
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of remote review by reviewer expertise type
evidence.effect: Radiologist reviewers: sensitivity 90%-95%, specificity 74%-84%, PPV 30%-42%; POCUS-certified EM reviewers: sensitivity 95%-98%, specificity 97%-100%, PPV 81%-100%.
evidence.quote: Performance is influenced by reviewer expertise.

evidence.title: Optimising the paradigms of human AI collaborative clinical coding
evidence.effect: Intern-HITL remained below AI-only despite +0.26 recall and +0.25 precision vs manual; senior-HITL reached 0.95 recall and 0.95 precision.
evidence.quote: However, compared to senior and junior coders who excelled on collaborative manner mode, the intern in HITL mode performed slightly worse than the AI-based coding system.

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Large Language Model-Augmented Diagnostic Reasoning in Thoracic Imaging: Impact of Radiologic Expertise
evidence.outcome: Rate of switching to incorrect diagnosis after misleading AI output by reader expertise
evidence.effect: Residents had a higher rate of switching to incorrect diagnoses after misleading LLM output than thoracic radiologists (60.6% vs 32.4%; p = .009).
evidence.quote: Residents, compared with thoracic radiologists, had a greater rate of accepting LLM-favored diagnoses (73.2% vs 48.9%; p < .001), including a greater rate of switching to an incorrect diagnosis after a misleading LLM output (60.6% vs 32.4%; p = .009).

evidence.title: Divergent impacts of explainable AI for dermatological diagnosis on clinicians versus lay people
evidence.effect: Medical students were more deferential than PCPs: role β = 0.067, P = 0.037; skin expertise β = 0.073, P = 0.005.
evidence.quote: We observed that the proportion of deferential participants was higher among medical students than PCPs (linear mixed model on the proportion of deferential participants, with medical role and medical expertise in skin as the main factor, controlling other confounders: main effect of medical role: β = 0.067, 95% CI: 0.004−0.130, P = 0.037; main effect of skin expertise: β = 0.073, 95% CI: 0.022−0.124, P = 0.005; Supplementary Table 25 ).

commentary.bottom_line: No study tests whether verifying licensure, role, or expertise before allowing use of AI outputs reduces misinterpretation or harm. Three offline hazard studies found that less experienced users deferred more to AI or performed worse with it than senior clinicians or coders, which suggests the hazard is real but does not show that credential restrictions correct it.

perspectives.view: No study compares restricted and unrestricted user access, so certainty for the practice is rated as no direct evidence. The three hazard studies are simulations or retrospective replays from three countries. Two used 9 coders and 10 readers, and one enrolled 1,096 participants. Their findings on expertise point the same way, but they describe the problem rather than test the safeguard.

After misleading LLM output, residents switched to an incorrect diagnosis in 60.6% of cases, compared with 32.4% for thoracic radiologists (p = .009). Medical students also deferred to AI more than primary care physicians did. These findings suggest that automation bias may be larger among trainees, although none of the studies measured patient outcomes.

In a coding simulation, intern coders working with AI stayed below AI-only performance, while senior coders working with AI reached 0.95 recall and 0.95 precision. This suggests that the value of human review may depend on reviewer skill. No study examined how role-based access controls perform in live workflows or how often users bypass them.

FDA draft guidance asks manufacturers to list the qualifications or clinical role of intended output interpreters, and a European pathology society paper reads the EU AI Act as requiring qualified supervision. These sources set labeling and deployer expectations. They do not supply evidence that enforcing those expectations changes outcomes.

In the coding study, intern coders working with AI stayed below AI-only performance, while senior coders working with AI reached 0.95 recall and 0.95 precision. If that pattern holds, restricting interpretation to senior personnel may shift workload toward a smaller and costlier group. No study reports staffing, cost, or throughput effects of such restrictions.

One hazard study was conducted with coders in China in a non-English setting. No study tested the practice in Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy settings. Restricting AI use to specialists could affect who receives AI-supported care in settings with few specialists, but no study has measured this.

commentary.research_gap: Prospective studies should compare outcomes when AI output interpretation is restricted by credential or role with outcomes when it is open to all clinicians, measuring diagnostic errors, patient harm, and access delays. Studies should also test whether training or competency checks for non-specialists can close the performance gap seen in the hazard studies.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. One hazard study involved a non-English coding setting in China, and none included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The effect of credential restrictions on care access in resource-limited settings therefore remains unknown.
